newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian party rocks coalition with plans to quit.
newsitem.headline: Indian party rocks coalition with plans to quit.

text.p: A regional Indian party said on Monday it planned to pull out of Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's fractious centre-left United Front coalition, sparking concerns over the government's stability.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party, to which Industry Minister Murasoli Maran belongs, said it planned to continue to support Gujral's government from outside, but cited differences over the conduct of some unnamed coalition partners.

There was no immediate threat to the government, which has been in power for less than three months. The DMK accounts for less than a tenth of the United Front's 178 seats in the 545-member lower house of parliament.

"The DMK is not willing to go along with the personal whims of some leaders and the private minimum programmes of certain parties," the party's president, Muthuvel Karunanidhi, said in a statement in Madras, capital of the state of Tamil Nadu.
"Until the situation improves, the DMK is planning to stay out of the ministry and support the government from outside," said Karunanidhi, who is also the state's chief minister.

Stock markets reacted nervously to the announcement. The Bombay Stock Exchange sensitive index tumbled 2.28 percent, closing provisionally at 4,223.61 points. Panic selling on the Delhi bourse drove its benchmark index down 3.3 percent to 891.56 points.

"The DMK's decision certainly worries us and is bound to create upheavals in the government," Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry president A.S. Kasliwal told the Press Trust of India.

The DMK statement gave no details, but party politicians said it was directed at the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), which has taken a hard line against admitting a breakaway political group of Gujral's Janata Dal party.

"Private minimum programme" apparently refers to CPI-M's hard line on not admitting the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD). When the coalition was formed, its disparate partners had agreed to sink differences under a "common minimum programme".
DMK officials said the main issue was CPI-M's attempts to force the RJD, formed earlier this month by ex- Janata Dal president Laloo Prasad Yadav, out of the coalition.

"We are angry with the communists who are unnecessarily creating complications," a state government minister told Reuters. "We believe the CPM is interfering too much in the affairs of the Janata Dal."
Yadav has refused calls led by the CPI-M to resign as chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar after federal police indicted him in a $280 million embezzlement scandal. He says he is innocent.

The CPI-M wants his group to be kept out of Gujral's coalition unless he resigns to face trial. Gujral has been hinting that Yadav should resign but has not agreed to sack three of his supporters from the federal ministry.
"The DMK is not able to appreciate the Laloo Prasad issue," CPI-M general secretary Harkishen Singh Surjeet said. "If we are lax on that, the BJP will gain."
"We cannot compromise on corruption," he said.
Surjeet told Reuters the crisis would blow over when he met Karunanidhi later this week.
"This thing will be sorted out on the 17th," he said.
But other coalition partners said they were apprehensive over the DMK's decision.
"It is a crisis that needs to be resolved," Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) president G.K. Moopanar told reporters. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram belongs to the TMC.
The main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) seized upon the disarray within the ruling alliance, calling the DMK's decision "political suicide".
The United Front's key ally, Congress, said the decision would not affect the government's stability and said its 140 deputies would continue to support Gujral's administration.
